about: Benchmark set for the Review desk judges: synthetic, labelled test data (no real papers, posts or people). 'credible' is the label a careful reader would give. Add items here when a mis-judgement is found; never edit an item to make a score pass.

items.title: Sample: Self-edited scaffolding on held-out coding tasks (test data)
items.text: We evaluated 3 agent variants on 500 held-out tasks. Compared with the baseline, the self-edited agent solved 41.2% versus 35.0% (95% confidence interval 3.9 to 8.5 points, across 5 seeds). An ablation keeps only 1.1 points without better test selection. Limitations: tasks are short and gains shrink after round three. Code is available at github.com/sample-org/sample-repo.

items.title: Sample: Sparse features in a toy transformer (test data)
items.text: We train sparse autoencoders on a 2-layer toy model and measure reconstruction on a held-out test set. Compared to a random-direction baseline, steering with the learned feature changes the target behaviour in 62% of 400 prompts versus 4% for the baseline (standard error 2.1 points). The effect fails on prompts longer than 128 tokens, a limitation we do not resolve. Weights are released.

items.title: Sample: What a new agent benchmark does and does not show (test data)
items.text: The evaluation covers 120 tasks with 3 runs each. The best model reaches 54% against a 31% baseline from last year, with error bars of about 4 points. Contamination is possible because some tasks are public, and the authors only test on short tasks, so the result does not show general autonomy.

items.title: Sample: comment asking for a baseline (test data)
items.text: The 18% gain is interesting, but it was measured on 50 prompts with no held-out set and no random baseline, so I would wait for a replication before reading much into it.

items.title: Sample: AGI is here, everything changes (test data)
items.text: This is the breakthrough no one is talking about. The new model achieved human-level reasoning and will soon surpass every expert. Superintelligence is inevitable and imminent. It is state-of-the-art on everything.

items.text: Recursive self-improvement has definitely started. The model rewrote itself overnight and is now superhuman. This is revolutionary and unprecedented.

items.title: Sample: Recursive self-improvement of toy research agents (test data)
items.text: We present a loop in which a research agent proposes changes to its own code, benchmarks each version on 12 tasks and keeps the best on hidden evaluations. Over 6 rounds it found 4 successive improvements. The gains transferred to 3 held-out benchmarks, where the best agent matches or exceeds a human-engineered baseline agent. Reward hacking fell from 40% to 25% of runs, a property the loop did not target.

items.title: Sample: Self-improving systems, a survey of 900 papers (test data)
items.text: We survey 900 papers from 2023 to 2026 on systems that improve themselves, and classify them by what is improved and how fully the loop is closed. We separate bounded self-refinement from open-ended self-improvement and order evaluation signals from formal verifiers to self-assessment. We find that reported gains follow this ordering, and that self-confirming loops explain most failures. Measurement of self-improvement for governance is the least studied area.

items.title: Sample: Self-improving AI is no longer sci-fi (test data)
items.text: Self-improving AI is the holy grail of the field, and the gap is closing fast. Labs say new models are now built largely by earlier ones. The coming intelligence explosion could be the most consequential event in history, a doomsday scenario for some and utterly transformative for others. Explosive progress is coming. Sources include posts on social media.

items.title: Sample: Agents fall short on open research questions, study finds (test data)
items.text: A study posted this week (arXiv 2611.00009) tested whether coding agents can answer the central question of two unpublished papers. Graded by the papers' own authors, the agents finished the engineering but made little progress on the research questions in either case. The authors list five recurring failure modes. Two case studies are a small sample, and the researchers say the result has not yet been tested on other fields. Whether agents will automate research remains an open question.

items.title: Sample: Why self-improving AI is already here (test data)
items.text: Self-improving AI is already here. Labs now build each model mostly with the previous one. Agents run their own experiments and improve their own code. Each generation makes the next one faster. This is how progress compounds. The next few model generations will automate most of AI research.
